theme: Numbers that compare: counting says who wins

activities.title: Which pile wins
activities.intro: Two piles are on the screen. Guess with your eyes which pile has more, then count with your finger to check. Tap the pile with more.
activities.offScreen: Go grab two handfuls of blocks, make two piles, and tell a grown-up which pile wins and how counting told you so.

rounds.prompt: Two piles of blocks. Tap the pile with more blocks.
Two piles of fish. Tap the pile with more fish.
Two piles of stars. Tap the pile with more stars.
So close! Count carefully. Tap the pile with more coins.

activities.title: Push them together
activities.intro: Two little groups meet and become one big group. Count them all, every single one. Tap how many altogether.
activities.offScreen: At dinner, put some spoons and some forks in one pile and count how many altogether, one number for each.

rounds.prompt: 4 red blocks and 3 blue blocks join into one pile. How many blocks altogether? Tap the number.
5 green leaves and 3 yellow leaves blow into one pile. How many leaves altogether? Tap the number.
6 purple flowers and 3 red flowers go into one vase. How many flowers altogether? Tap the number.
6 blue fish and 4 orange fish swim into one group. How many fish altogether? Tap the number.

activities.title: Which pile has fewer
activities.intro: Now the sneaky one. The piles are almost the same, so eyes are not enough. Count both piles, then tap the pile with fewer.
activities.offScreen: Make two sock piles that are almost the same, count them both, and tell a grown-up which pile has fewer.

rounds.prompt: Two piles of cups, almost the same. Tap the pile with fewer cups.
Two flocks of birds. Count them both! Tap the flock with fewer birds.
Two bunches of flowers, so close. Tap the bunch with fewer flowers.
Last one, the closest of all. Tap the pile with fewer triangles.

parentCard.title: Sock towers from the laundry
steps: At laundry time, build two sock towers together, one of 6 socks and one of 4.
Ask which tower is taller. Let them guess by looking first, then count each tower out loud together, one number for one sock.
Ask the big question: 6 beats 4, but by how many? Take socks off the tall tower one at a time, counting each one, until the two towers match.
Swap jobs: they build two towers of their own choosing and quiz you, and you sometimes guess wrong on purpose so they can catch you by counting.
notice: Do they count each sock exactly once, one number for one sock, even past 6?
When the towers are close, do they count to decide, or still trust their eyes?
Can they say the winner with numbers, like 6 beats 4 by 2?
